CHAIR ( Senator Marielle Smith ): I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today, and I pay my respects to their elders past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people joining us today.

The committee has fixed 21 November 2025 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial position of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees, unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Dr Jess Walsh, Minister for Early Childhood Education and Minister for Youth, representing the Minister for Education. Minister, do you have an opening statement this morning?

Senator Walsh: I do not.

CHAIR: Mr Cook, do you have an opening statement?

Mr Cook : I don't have an opening statement, but I have a few clarifications about acting arrangements for the committee's information. Ms Jasna Blackwell is Acting Deputy Secretary of Corporate Enabling Services today. Mr Markovic had long leave posted and is running the Chicago marathon, and we wish him all the best with that. We normally, every estimates—

Senator DOLEGA: While we are sitting at a desk! Is that to make us feel bad about ourselves?

CHAIR: As we sit in a room for 15 hours a day.

Mr Cook : I'm sure he's watching as he's jogging. Ms Karen Sandercock will be Acting Deputy Secretary for Higher Education, Research and International, acting for Mr Ben Rimmer as he has been appointed as the Director-General of Housing Group and has moved across to Treasury. You'll see that, at the back row, we've got a whole group of graduates that we've brought to estimates, as part of their yearlong program with us, to watch the accountability and transparency process in action. If there are any hard questions for me, I'll get the graduates to come to the table and answer those for you.

CHAIR: If we get bored, we might call them ourselves. Just joking! You'll be fine. Enjoy! It is lovely to have you all here, and thank you for that update. We'll now dive into questions relating to corporate and enabling services. Senator Duniam.

Senator DUNIAM: That is a cruel and unusual punishment—bringing the graduates to this—but good luck for the day. I want to go to the aim of the government, or the department, in response to what happened in Victoria—the revelations arising out of the Joshua Dale Brown case—and the intention to conduct more spot checks in childcare centres. There was a desire, or at least a commitment, to have more staff in the department assigned specifically to those checks. Have more staff been brought on to do that work?

Mr Cook : Yes, the government has made that decision. The details of that will be in next budgetary papers, but more staff have been brought on as a result of that. In fact, we are in the process of training our staff in relation to that matter. Minister Clare and Minister Walsh indicated at the last Education Ministers Meeting that it is the intention that those spot checks will first start in November this year.

Senator DUNIAM: In November this year?

Mr Cook : That's right.

Senator DUNIAM: So how many additional staff have been brought on?

Mr Cook : We've been given a number by the government. We're in the process of recruitment at the moment. The early childhood team will be able to tell us in the early childhood outcome how many are on—

Senator DUNIAM: We'll come back to them.

Mr Cook : but we're in the process of recruitment and, as I said, there are staff that we are currently training. I can give you the details of the numbers.

Senator DUNIAM: Yes, let's go to the numbers then, and we'll deal with the details. How many are you allocated to bring on?

Mr Cook : The early childhood team will have that. Off the top of my head—the only reason I'm saying that is that I don't have the details in front of me—I think it's around 80.

Senator DUNIAM: Eighty additional.

Mr Cook : But I will say that that could be corrected by the early childhood team when they're here.

Senator DUNIAM: That's alright. We can check that when they're here. I just thought that, under corporate, if it was a provision provided through the budget process, you would have a general sense of it here.

Mr Cook : I do, but I'm also not pre-empting what government would publish in their budgetary papers, which they would do through the MYEFO process, rather than now.

Senator DUNIAM: It'd be included in that?

Mr Cook : That's right. It was after budget, so, in terms of budget updates, it's normally in the MYEFO papers that that information would be made public by the government.

Senator DUNIAM: We might, then, come back to the details around that in the childcare section. That's fine.

Mr Cook : Sure. That's no problem at all.

Senator DUNIAM: Then, in relation to the allocation of $189 million in funding to childcare safety, has any of that been partly or fully offset by changes to other elements of the education budget?

Mr Cook : Again, that's budget-in-confidence information, but I can say to you that the answer to that is no.

Senator DUNIAM: That is a good answer. Fair enough. I might, then, turn quickly to regulation. As I understand it, the department has brought in roughly 130 new regulations since the change of government. Is that a number you're familiar with?

Mr Cook : It's not, but I'll accept that number.

Senator DUNIAM: Sure. You're very trusting, aren't you! The minister may not be so trusting of numbers I throw at you. It was work done by the Parliamentary Library that I think Senator Bragg has tabled in a number of estimates. Do you have a rough understanding of what those 130 regulations that have been brought in since the new government took office would cover?

Mr Cook : Do you mean in the last couple of months?

Senator DUNIAM: No, in the last three years and a couple of months.

Mr Cook : So it's since 2022?

Senator DUNIAM: Yes.

Mr Cook : I would anticipate the large majority of those regulations would impact in the higher education space, looking at things like gender based violence and at some of the issues that universities have faced in that area. They're the sorts of areas that I would anticipate, but I haven't seen the Parliamentary Library report, no.

Senator DUNIAM: Does this department run any sort of process to see what regulatory burden arises, beyond the regulatory impact statement you do prior to the introduction. Is there anything that the department does with stakeholders on the way through the implementation to see what burden is imposed?

Mr Cook : You beat me to it, because I was going to talk about regulatory impact statements.

Senator DUNIAM: I knew you were. That's why I mentioned it!

Mr Cook : You beat me to it, so thank you for that. Obviously, we do consult with the sector broadly across the range of things that government may choose to do in terms of legislation and the implementation of regulatory matters. If you look at the higher education space, one of the things that was a recommendation out of the Universities Accord, which will be one of the responsibilities of the new ATEC, is to actually look at the regulatory burden on the higher education space, for example.

In terms of other things, the regulatory burden for schools and early childhood from a Commonwealth perspective is minimal, because we don't regulate schools and early childhood services, as you know, so the regulatory posture of my department is quite small. In terms of what I do from a regulatory perspective—and you can see this online; I think it's on the Department of Finance website—when the Treasurer and the finance minister wrote to me and asked me to outline my regulatory responsibilities and how I might reduce some of the regulatory burden, it's really quite minimal. I will have and I am establishing, of course, the gender based violence regulatory unit, the national code of which was passed in parliament. Other than that, our regulatory burden from a department perspective is minimal.

Senator DUNIAM: We will come back to this when we talk more higher education and what the ATEC may do, but, in terms of the department's assessment of any impacts on productivity, is that part of what you do with stakeholders? Is that a specific metric you look at?

Mr Cook : It's not a metric per se, but it's certainly something we discuss with our range of stakeholders. Again, the Treasurer and the finance minister asked me, as the accountable authority, to look at the impact of regulation in relation to productivity. You can find my written response in relation to that on the Department of Finance website.

Senator DUNIAM: That's fine. I won't go further there. I should have mentioned earlier that there was a letter the opposition did send the department with some questions. Was there a response forthcoming?

Mr Cook : I think we've got something we can table this morning.

Senator DUNIAM: That would be excellent. While they are doing that, we might move on to other matters. When we receive a copy of what is to be tabled, I will probably come back to that through the normal process. Are we able to get an understanding of the total amount of funding spent in 2024-25 on programs administered in whole or even in part across the education portfolio, both on and off budget, respectively?

Mr Cook : That will be in that. I have the letter right in front of me. We don't have anything we would define as off budget. All of our expenditure, all of our financials—and the chief financial officer is here if you need clarification—are effectively outlined in our budget papers. In terms of the total amount spent in 2024-25—was that—

Senator DUNIAM: Yes, that's correct.

Mr Cook : It was $61.454 billion. That is both the department and our portfolio agencies, with all of that being on budget. That's question 4(a).

Senator DUNIAM: And expenditure so far is part b.

Mr Cook : Expenditure so far this financial year is $12.078 billion.

Senator DUNIAM: Okay. Do we have a value of how much money has been spent across the department and its agencies on consultants and contractors in the last 3½ years since 2022?

Mr Cook : We will have it for the department.

Senator DUNIAM: Whatever you have.

Mr Cook : I'll see if we can help you on that. I don't think we'll have agencies, because they're their own accountable authorities, but we'll have the department's CFO to help us on that.

Mr Boyd : I have the figures for the financial year to date and last financial year's spend on contractors. I'd also have that for consultants, but not back to 2022.

Senator DUNIAM: That's fine. We might do that part on notice. If you want to go through what you have, that would be excellent.

Mr Boyd : Certainly. For the 2025-26 financial year through to the end of July 2025, the department spent $1.15 million on contractors. For the 2024-25 financial year, the department spent $13.38 million on the contractors for the whole of the last financial year.

Mr Cook : As you can see, we are not big spenders in this space at all.

Senator DUNIAM: That goes to Defence or other places like that.

Mr Cook : And we have a very small contractor workforce as well.

Mr Boyd : Consultancy for this financial year through to 31 July 2025 is $4½ million and for the last financial year was $13.35 million.

Senator DUNIAM: Is there anywhere in the department, in terms of the public interface webpage or similar, where the public might be able to see a consolidated list of all spending measures from within the department and its portfolio agencies?

Mr Boyd : The portfolio budget statements do set out by measure the government's decisions in relation to spending. There was an estimate of those—a budget instead of financial statements as part of the PBS. The annual financial statements will capture that in aggregate—

Senator DUNIAM: But not by line item.

Mr Boyd : Not by line item. There is a part of the annual report where agencies are required to disclose the top five, or 10 or so spends for contracts and things like that just to give a bit more detail. That is in the annual report each year. That requirement came in a couple of years ago, so it doesn't give the full list, but it gives the sense of 'Here are the top spends for contracts and consultancies.'

Senator DUNIAM: Alright. I will examine that further, and I'm sure we'll be able talk about that in December when we will be back here doing this all over again, which we are all excited about. Is there a summary available of the savings measures that have been made within the department over the last 12 months? While we're looking at that, what is intended to be marked for saving over the next 12?

Mr Boyd : It is only a summary in that, as governments make decisions, it's included in each PBS. In terms of the most recent decision of government, we've been advised of the amount for the current financial year 2025-26. The government hasn't yet made decisions on future years or advised us of those decisions.

Senator DUNIAM: Yes, like 2026-27—of course.

Mr Boyd : So, certainly for the current financial year for the department, it's $5.43 million.

Mr Cook : And they are in the areas you are aware of—things like travel et cetera—so we have made decisions around reductions in those areas and we monitor that effectively on a fortnightly basis.

Senator DUNIAM: Okay. Could I go to the capability needs review please. What did that review, which, of course, was completed earlier in the year, conclude was most in need of reform within the department? What was the highlight of the review in terms of what was in most need of reform within the department?

Mr Cook : There were effectively four things outlined in the review. These are public; they're in the review report. The first one was for us to continue to deliver a holistic education strategy as the national education department. There was a view from the reviewers that we needed to do more work around the stewardship of that and how we work states and territories and our stakeholders—universities, childcare providers—in the work that we do around education. We had already done some work around that which we called the long-term direction, which was outlining for the department, effectively, what we do to support the government in realising better education for Australians, so there's work already done on that. Basically we have continued to develop that strategy.

The second one was to further enhance the collaboration with our external stakeholders. As you would appreciate, in our department the federation plays a big role; there is a lot of federated work we do with states and territories in the school space and in the early childhood space. There's the work that we do with the First Nations key stakeholders. SNAICC and NATSIACC are the national bodies for education and early childhood education. There are universities. There's the range of stakeholders and enhancing our collaboration with them in the work that we do.

The next one was to monitor and influence the transparent sharing of data, which is really important, across all areas of the portfolio. Again, part of this is about federated models and also about legislation, and you note that one of the things the minister introduced yesterday in the House was legislation which enables us to have better sharing around the childcare data that we had. We want to be able to do that so that we can actually learn from what the data says, what the trend says, to inform our policy work, and it is the same with schools and universities. The third thing said that we should continue to influence the transparent sharing of data, which means I'm having conversations with my state peers about how state data could be available to us and Commonwealth data could be available to the states to inform some of that.

The last one was increasing workforce skills, knowledge and regulation around the slightly changing nature of the department and the fact that we are delivering programs and we are now becoming regulators. The department has traditionally been known as a policy department; we develop policy. We haven't traditionally been specific regulators, but, if you look at the work that's happening around gender based violence and some of the compliance work that we'll do in child care, we just need to make sure our staff have the skills to enable them to deliver those requirements as well. So they were the four main findings that came out of the report.

Senator DUNIAM: In terms of the implementation of responses to that review, how do you report on what you're achieving?

Mr Cook : There's an action plan which we developed, which has been published, so that's a publicly available action plan. In that action plan, we list how we're going to measure our success in relation to those things.

Senator DUNIAM: And the measurements of success are published at points in time, over the course of time?

Mr Cook : They will be, through our corporate plan. The corporate plan will reflect on the work that we do. We talk about how we'll measure success by establishing a baseline of the department's capabilities, capturing feedback from stakeholders and tracking key census results, which are public anyway. It's in the report. I'm happy to read them out, but it's in the publicly available report.

Senator DUNIAM: If it's there, I will be able to go and have a look there at regular points in time. How long do I have, Chair?

CHAIR: You're the only one seeking the call for this one.

Senator DUNIAM: I'll churn through. I won't be too long, I hope, depending on answers of course. If we can go to some tendering issues, then, I just want to go to some contracts that the department had. I'll do it by number: CN4152496 and CN4153504. I would normally ask how on earth you come up with these numbers, but I'm not going to today.

Mr Cook : I think they're generated by the system, actually.

Mr Boyd : That's right—the whole-of-government system, AusTender. Some people have a list—we've got an electronic list—of all the contract numbers. They're just searching through it as we speak. We'll be able to get a quick copy then, so it might just take a moment or two, and we can determine which part of the organisation is best able to respond to the questions.

Senator DUNIAM: If not here. Understood.

Mr Boyd : If it's not in corporate. That's right.

Senator DUNIAM: We can ad lib while we're waiting. One was $102,000 for two months of scribing work for a recruitment round, and the other was $45,000 for 40 days of work by a computer programmer. Does that accord with the information you've got there?

Mr Cook : Yes.

Senator DUNIAM: With regard to the one relating to the scribing work, can I understand what position, or positions, that recruitment round related to?

Mr Cook : That's related to my early childhood group. Those contracts are signed off by the relevant FAS, the first assistant secretary, in early childhood, so I don't have knowledge of this one. Early childhood are this afternoon and should be able to help you with that, or we can take it on notice if it's easier for you.

Senator DUNIAM: Okay, we'll come back. Why don't you take it on notice, and we'll come back. One way or another, we'll get to the bottom of it.

Mr Cook : It might have been a series of rounds as well. Often we have over 200 or 300 people applying for some of these positions, so it might have been work in relation to that. My early childhood people are watching, so we'll put them on alert, but you'll come back and ask the question, if that's okay.

Senator DUNIAM: You probably don't have any more detail. I was going to see how many scribes were engaged under the tender, but you won't know that either.

Mr Cook : No, I've just got a description and how much it was. That's all I've got in front of me, I'm afraid.

Senator DUNIAM: Is that sort of contract something that you regularly would pay for?

Mr Cook : It depends on the size of the recruitment round that we're doing. I just don't know what this—it might have been for the worker retention payment work, where we needed many, many people employed for it. That might be the reason for this, but, again, I will have to rely on my early childhood team to cover this.

Senator DUNIAM: That's fine; we'll come back to that. We may be done sooner than we thought on corporate, which is unheard of in this place. In terms of decisions made to procure these services, is there not a capability within the department to offer scribing to support executive teams or recruitment teams or whoever is doing the work?

Mr Cook : Again, it depends on the nature of the recruitment that we're looking at. If we had to tie some staff up for a month or so for this pure purpose—

Senator DUNIAM: Yes, it could.

Mr Cook : we may make the decision that we wouldn't do that because of the nature of the work that has to happen. It really is case by case when they make the decisions in relation to that.

Senator DUNIAM: Well that being the case, we'll come back to that with some of those more detailed questions. I presume the decision-maker will be one of the witnesses.

Mr Cook : I would absolutely assume so as well.

Senator DUNIAM: Excellent. We can come to the high-level details later on. The other tender—we might have the same issue here—related to the computer programmer. As I understand it, the contract notice shows that across 30 business days it was around $1,500 a day that was paid for the services of this computer programmer, and I assume it was a single programmer, not a team of them.

Mr Cook : Mr McDonald came back, so that's useful.

Mr McDonald : This contract was in my division. I'm afraid I don't have before me a lot of details on the contract, but I believe it's part of the work we have been doing which is around enhancing our capability to understand the behavioural impacts of childcare policy changes. We've been doing a bit of work to enhance that capability. As part of a lot of our work, we do some sophisticated data analysis—I guess that's how I'd describe it—and that does require programming in R, the language—

Senator DUNIAM: Yes, I've learnt this. I had to figure out what R was.

Mr McDonald : We do have a set of internal capabilities for programming in R, but sometimes we need to get in extra capability, and that does come at a cost.

Senator DUNIAM: I don't know what R is, I'm happy to admit. You have internal capability. What then drove the need for external servicing?

Mr Cook : We don't have capability in that software language. I think that's the point Mr McDonald was making.

Mr McDonald : Sometimes it's partly to surge on what we can deliver.

Senator DUNIAM: It's a surge thing? Okay. You're saying it was a surge because—

Mr McDonald : I think it's a surge, yes.

Senator DUNIAM: I don't know what the market's like, but I presume, in procuring this service in accordance with the rules of procurement, you went to market and tested a number of—

Mr McDonald : I don't have the details on which exact process we went through, but we would have gone through the process that ensure PGPA value for money.

Senator DUNIAM: I'll probably end up putting all of these on notice, for what it's worth, but, with the process of procurement, do you go and look at what the standard market rate is? Is that one of the considerations that the department has in its decision-making process for procurement, or is it a case of literally who is best to do what we need when we need it?

Mr Boyd : It probably depends on the type of procurement. By that I mean that there are some requirements to use mandatory whole-of-government panels, so for consultancy-type projects there is a whole-of-government panel for a range of people services. There is a whole-of-government panel, and it's mandatory for departments to utilise those panels. The normal process would be that you would approach entities on the panel. They've all been pre-vetted by the Department of Finance and have met all the requirements. You would approach several of those and put your work requirement to them, see what rate or total they come back with and then follow the steps for value for money, noting that price isn't always the only determinant of value for money.

Sometimes you might also do a true request for tender, where you go to the market directly. That's usually for larger or more complex or larger-value-type procurements where, again, there's a set of rules under the Commonwealth Procurement Rules and the PGPA Act that specify how that's to be conducted, and then you go to the market and invite people to tender a response to the requirement you put out there. So it's different depending on the procurement.

Dr Russell : But I would also note that, as part of the consultation that the Department of Education is currently conducting on the TEQSA Act, we support the fact that the question has been raised about whether TEQSA should continue the routine mandated accreditation of courses for non-self-accrediting providers or whether there are other ways to achieve the desired results. So there are initiatives that potentially may flow from that consultation that are also targeted to regulatory burden, and that would be a potential change in the legislation for us.

Senator SHARMA: Does TEQSA have a statement of expectations currently in effect that the minister has issued to you, of a kind that other regulatory agencies have, about the appropriate focus and balance and priorities?

Dr Russell : That process is live, and when it is concluded we will also have the appropriate response to that. I expect that will be published in the usual way.

Senator SHARMA: So there's no current statement of expectations?

Dr Russell : There has not been one historically, but there is one in development.

Senator SHARMA: When would you expect that to be—this year?

Dr Russell : I would defer to the minister, as effectively the expectations come from the minister and we make commitments in response.

Senator SHARMA: But it is ongoing? You have been involved in conversations—

Dr Russell : It is live, yes.

Senator SHARMA: Thank you. I don't have any further questions, but my colleague does.

Senator KOVACIC: I have a couple of questions on your work on managing external actors. Can you quantify how many of your staff have been assigned to that project and over what period of time, and do you have any data on the financial costs to date of that project or of that work?

Dr Russell : I say with a wry smile that we did that on the smell of an oily rag as part of our non-BAU, over the cap of normal business response to the protests and encampments. We have a policy team of, I think, two people. One of the things we committed to the sector and to the minister when there were protest encampments, and challenges that that gave rise to on campus, was that we would share best practice with the sector. We did a number of things. We drew from our own learnings of how universities had responded to issues, and we held a series of roundtables with the sector. We did a variety of things, including capturing the sector's learning and expertise about what it had needed to do to respond to external actors. We have pulled that together and consulted on that. It won't be a statement of expectations on that particular issue, because that was deemed too prescriptive in terms of some of the things that were shared as best practice, such as the wearing of body cams and some things that may be fit for purpose in some circumstances but not others. We anticipate that we will shortly publish that as a sector alert, sector information, so that that's accessible to the sector. It would not even be half an FTE for any period of time. We do a lot with very little.

Senator KOVACIC: It sounds like it. Was your job made harder or complicated by the fact that there was a little bit of resistance? Well, there wasn't a little bit; there was quite intense criticism at times from some universities on the interim guidance. Was it made more challenging for you, or was it a piece of work that you were determined to do?

Dr Russell : We responded to that in a way that was entirely novel for the sector. I expected a degree of caution about TEQSA weighing in early and proactively and developing our response in the way that we did. However, we had exceptionally strong cooperation from the sector. When we received feedback, both on the draft statement of regulatory expectation on grievances and complaints and also on what was at that stage proposed as a statement of expectations about managing external actors, we had some quite opposing views in relation to the expectations around complaints processes. We had to weigh those up because students and student representative groups in some instances had very different views and expectations from what universities and providers did. And universities and non-university providers had different views. We accepted the reasons that the sector was uneasy about our sharing in a prescriptive way some of the practices about managing external actors. Accordingly, we will still share the information, but we will do it in a different format that has different implications for how it will be implemented by universities.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. This is either to the minister or to TEQSA. Have you formally analysed international examples of higher education regulation to determine whether the TEQSA model is best practice or if there are any changes or adjustments we could make? If you have, what did you find?

Dr Russell : In relation to changes to the TEQSA legislation that are proposed?

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, or in terms of how the model operates—it would obviously then require legislative amendment—and getting an understanding of whether the model itself fits best practice for what we are doing.

Dr Russell : We do a few things to stay in touch with regulatory practice. One is that we have regular contact with international counterparts. We would often video at odd hours of the day and night, and we would have a Teams call with regulators to understand initiatives in practice. We share a lot of hours through the GAIN, the Global Academic Integrity Network. We also actively participate in the National Regulators Community of Practice events to understand diversity of regulatory practice as it applies in Australia. We actively engage with our stakeholders because every regulatory context is very different, so hearing from peak bodies, from students and from our provider stakeholders helps us to critique and improve our model.

In the development of our regulatory strategy, we are very public and transparent. One of the objectives of that is to be more transparent about how we go about our regulatory work. We've scheduled a workshop after our conference, to which we've invited all providers in the sector and students to contribute to members. So we do a range of things to pick up local as well as national and international good practice and really work that into the way that we are developing our strategy and our change.
